By the way, when Stewart played Prospero in "The Tempest", it premiered in the summer of 1995 at the Delacorte Theater in Central Park (more popularly known as 'Shakespeare in the Park'), only later transferring to Broadway three months later.

Although he had more of a supporting role in "Conspiracy Theory", one with comedic moments as a sinister "bad guy", that movie is one of this NYC native's favorites!

They don't actually need the full $6.3 Billion: About $2.7 billion to $3 billion of the stolen funds were in stablecoins (like USDT and USDC) or specific tokens. Issuer companies like Tether and Circle, along with various network councils, were able to quickly freeze those funds on-chain, effectively blocking the hackers from using them. That reduces the actual "unrecovered" loss down to roughly $3.3 billion to $3.6 billion.

The Emergency Fund (SAFU): Binance maintains a dedicated emergency insurance pool called the SAFU (Secure Asset Fund for Users). It currently holds about 15,000 Bitcoin, which is 'worth' around $1.1 billion to $1.2 billion.

Corporate Treasury & Other Assets: The SAFU fund only covers about a third of the remaining un-frozen loss. To cover the rest, Binance’s co-founder Changpeng Zhao ("CZ") stated they will tap into Binance's corporate revenues and operational reserves. He even publicly hinted at liquidating or leveraging other corporate investments, such as their billion-dollar equity stake in SpaceX, if necessary.

Marx underestimated culture, and Nietzsche underestimated economics. Together, they paint a more coherent picture of what is going wrong in the world today.

Marx warned us that the form of capitalism from his era would not be sustainable for much longer, and Nietzsche warned us about the dangers of nihilism and the importance of creating new values.

The Oligarchs of big business are expecting to privatize all of the productivity gains of AI -- cutting the human labor cost with AI -- and socializing the costs and risks. 

Yesterday Microsoft announced that it was offering buyouts (and eventually layoffs?) a mind boggling 60 thousand employees. The company no longer needs humans to write and debug computer code the old-fashioned way. Microsoft will keep all of the productivity gains, and employees (and society) will have to deal with the consequences.

This trend may be inevitable. But suppose a new social contract is instituted whereby most of the productivity gains must accrue to labor in the form of shorter working hours with annual incomes remaining constant? This could mean that more human labor goes into such currently unpaid (but arguably much more important) work, e.g. more quality time for caring for children and the aged, building deeper human relationships, and stronger communities?

This would mean that, in the future, AI companies may not enjoy all of the benefits of displacing human labor. This should reduce valuations significantly. 

But the investment banks, VC investors and AI companies are using old obsolete business models to project valuations for an entirely transformed future.

This IPO can go forward as a business proposition only because the long adverse "tail risks" cannot exceed the initial investment. Society's huge risks are borne by us.

Why do these companies get to foist these risks on us?

If that happens in large numbers without a concomitant growth in jobs elsewhere in the economy, what exactly are those people supposed to do instead? 

We will still live in a world where humans are expected to ‘pull their weight’ and earn a living from work that is both satisfying and lucrative enough to pay the ever increasing costs of life today. Corporations that adopt the technology are not going to reduce the prices for their products and services when those things are cheaper to produce using AI, they’re going to pad their bottom line, and the few remaining white collar jobs left in those companies are going to do likewise. 

There have been proposals and experiments with offering minimum monthly salaries to people, paid for by the government, but those are fraught with potential drawbacks not least of which is that instead of lifting boats on the proverbial rising tide such handouts may instead have the effect of maintaining a population at a subsistence level of existence from which there is no escape.

comments.name: Rebecca Frankel
comments.body: The "bitter lesson" mythology was built on a misunderstanding. There was a long standing relationship between Silicon Valley and academia, in particular the MIT computer science department. That's because in previous cycles academia had built the infrastructure that made Silicon Valley people rich. The dot.com boom was built on two pieces of infrastructure, the Internet and the World Wide Web, both of whose leaders were at MIT by the time of the boom. So there was naturally the expectation that the next big thing would come out of MIT. So around 2012 when Silicon Valley started in on developing something new, they looked at what MIT people were doing, expecting to build on it. Instead, they fairly quickly overtook and superseded it. Being full of self-regard, they took this as a corroboration of their strategy. But there was something they didn't know: the "bitter lesson" people were not the culture at MIT that would have designed the next infrastructure layer. In 2001 Bush appointed a mini-Musk to DARPA who fired career program managers. The people they had overtaken were  doing not what their own judgement would have dictated, but instead what they funding agency's priorities forced them into. It was short-term focused and poorly funded.  Al Gore's tradition of generous support for infrastructure development was voted out by the hanging chads. In other words, Gore invented the Internet, but Dubya invented AI.

Sometimes the errors are minor. Sometimes they mishear or misunderstand the source. Sometimes their hands can't take notes as quickly as someone speaks, or their shorthand breaks down when they're writing their story. Other times, entirely new words are attributed to you that you did not say. 

People who are quoted by reporters with any regularity know this firsthand. 

I think it is more likely than not that Ms. Holmes was misquoted.

I'm essentially Creole and visited New Orleans frequently as a child and saw a bit of Creole culture back then. My mother, who grew up in New Orleans in the mid-Twentieth Century under Jim Crow, knew only a few odd phrases of Creole, but her grandmother (my great grandmother) spoke it fluently according to family lore. 

Now in my late middle age, it's interesting to finally hear some spoken Creole in this clip.

And incidentally, I see some comments here about the Cajun language and culture that conflate it with Creole. They're not the same thing. It was one of my mother's pet peeves that people often conflated them.

To the best of my knowledge, the Cajun people are descendants of refugees from Canada who settled primarily in rural Louisiana and spoke a language that's either a dialect of French or closely related to French. They are primarily white-identifying and did not, to the best of my knowledge, suffer under Jim Crow.

Conversely, the Creole people are multiethnic with significant African ancestry and, as noted in this article, were in some cases racially ambiguous and often did suffer under Jim Crow. The Creole people were also centered primarily in urban areas, especially New Orleans and Mobile.

comments.name: DarcieD
comments.body:
The rifampin was the only appropriate drug  for this victim of pharma and mental health providers pretending to care when all they do is throw meds. 

Antidepressants have never been shown effective for mild-moderate depression, and don't work for most people for severe depression. Hence, the admissions to hospital to stay safe when the MDD is so severe that suicidal ideation is prominent. When people get out of inpatient, inappropriate drugs are thrown at them. 

The treatment for MDD? talk therapy, especially the evidence-baed CBT for Depression. 

For anxiety? Talk therapy, expecially CBT. 

FOR INSOMNIA? Not sleeping pills, that's a fact. The tx that is FIRST LINE since 2006 (Amer Acad Sleep Med) is CBT-I, a very specific form of CBT that is based on the science of sleep medicine evidence. 

Sleeping pills? They may help a few people with transient (short term) insomnia who take the drug that's appropriate to the type of insomnia (short term, either can't get to sleep, or can't stay asleep, or wake too early and don't get back to sleep), if taken every single night for about a month. Otherwise, they do  NOT work, not for chronic insomnia, and not for most people. The patients I've seen for chronic insomnia typically suffered from the disorder for over 10 years. They'd been on multiple sleeping pills, sometimes every drug on the market. The average rating from patients, for efficacy of each drug tried? 2%. TWO percent efficacy. CBT efficacy? over 80%.

In fact, the Aztecs has a peculiar form of extractive empire: they actually didn't want to totally conquer the neighboring tribes they frequently defeated; their purpose in battle was twofold: to earn more feathers in their headdresses as symbols of bravery, and to capture prisoners they could first brutally sacrifice to their gods, and then eat.

Some historians and anthropologists have argued that, in spite of the highly ritualistic nature of how their priests killed their captives, the deeper underlying motivation for their cannibalism was really protein deficiency in the local food options. I once got into a rather heated argument with a former anthropology student who vehemently denied this, he claimed Aztec cannibalism was purely ritualistic, that properly cooked corn could compensate for their lack of other protein sources. I still think their lacking even chickens (the most common animal protein source throughout the world) was an important factor.

By the way, entomologists have discovered that cockroaches are cannibalistic, will eagerly eat other roaches -- but not members of their own families (yes, roaches live in families). 

Cannibalism is an interesting but repulsive subject.

Add some perspective on this.  The storage systems are thermal storage which can be used for industrial heat--such as cooking ethanol vats.

The Antora systems have a capacity about 50 MW of power...and about 5,000 MWh of thermal energy capacity.  The could be scaled up fairly somewhat.  Essentially can provide heat to make steam for what ever process.  If the steam is used to make electricity, a steam turbine would be about 35% efficient....so about 1,750 MWhr of electricity could be produced assuming no real drop in steam temperature during drain down.

The biggie:  11MWh thermal per acre of land...so to get to 5000 MWh for a system, it would be about 450 acres of land or 0.75 square miles.

Any storage system for energy will always be net negative.  More energy is put in than will be returned back...that is entropy.  So, this is not an energy supply system--it is net negative, but will take advantage of oversupply of wind and solar. 

They claim a 20 plus life cycle...that is a bit low unfortunately.

I’m reminded of an attack method from decades back, on a very secure piece of software.  The attack only asked the software to do valid operations, but was still able to crash many of the systems.  How?  By guessing what hardware the software was running on and making repeated operations that caused part of that hardware to overheat.

How much do you trust the information you receive? Do you know who filters it, how, and to what extent before it reaches you?

One of Russia’s most serious problems is its entrenched power structure, which resists change while constantly reshaping the country to preserve its own power.

If information is selected and distorted to serve those in power, even the highest leader may find himself making decisions within a reality constructed by others, believing he sees the world as it truly is.

President Putin must not rely solely on intelligence reports. He needs independent, open channels of communication to understand how the world is actually changing.

He must constantly question the accuracy of the information he receives and consider the possibility that his own judgments are wrong.

Blind loyalty slowly destroys people. It robs those who offer it of independent judgment and those who receive it of the opportunity to hear the truth.

A national leader needs not countless people who agree with him, but people who can tell him when he is wrong.

Back in the day, a novel came out.  "The Octopus."  

It was about the enormous power wielded by trusts and monopolies.  Reaching out those grasping tentacles--

--squeezing the  life out of American democracy!

And reading this article, I thought of Mr. Trump and the people who serve him. 

BUT--

--more than any other entity in American society, the courts and those indomitable judges who preside in them--

--have put up roadblocks to the Trumpian bulldozers.  

My stars! but the Trump people must hate these guys.  

And so,they resort to their tried 'n' true weapon--

--the derogatory label.  

"Rogue activist judges."  Neatly put!  

"Rogue" signifying men (and women) that have strayed beyond the prescribed limits. Running wild, so to speak.  

And "activist" suggesting--what?   Some private ideology, manufactured out of thin air.  Some gallimaufry of whims and prejudices no one need take seriously.

Guess what, you incorrigible Trumpians?  

They're still judges.  Duly constituted judges empowered to pronounce upon any and all cases brought before them.   

And oh yes!  

To say whatever they feel impelled to say. 

It's you guys and no one else! who are the lawless ones.  Rogue politicians if you will.  Urged on by a rogue president.

And I hope, I pray our judiciary remains what it has been.  

A bulwark of American democracy.  

And right now--

--virtually the only one we have. 

Thanks, Mr. Liptak

I haven’t read the book, but the reviewer seems just as ambivalent about the merits of CrossFit as the author, and just as taken in with the mystique.

Shared suffering is the secret sauce of CrossFit, just like going through boot camp with someone, or enduring a fraternity hazing together: you’re now friends for life.

CrossFit has done a world of good for the world of fitness, staring with barbells, kettlebells, and gymnastic movements like pull-ups and muscle-ups, but it has always leaned heavily into suffering and pushing beyond comfortable and healthy boundaries. 

If you have to puke in the middle of your workout you’re now a member of the club. Blow out your shoulder on that 67th overhead press? Now you’re getting somewhere! 

But salient thing about Greg Glassman’s supposedly offhand remark about George Floyd is not that it revealed what a racist and arrogant jerk he is, but how much it reflects the actual political sentiments of much of the CrossFit world. 

Every CrossFit gym in the country has a giant American flag on the wall, probably a Gadsen flag (“Don’t tread on me”), and if you’re lucky, a Confederate flag, because Southern Pride, of course. Big law enforcement and ex-military membership. Big white, tattooed, gun-toting membership. CrossFit  culture was MAGA before MAGA was even a thing.  

There’s more than meets the eye with CrossFit, both good and bad. I guess we’ll have to read the book.

comments.name: Nag Madamanc

India needs a strong privacy law to protect its citizens, but privacy must not become a shield for those in power. By omitting explicit protections for journalism and potentially allowing government agencies to obtain newsroom data or restrict access to public records, this law risks weakening the very accountability a democracy needs.

Under Modi, concerns about press freedom, concentrated media ownership, and pressure on independent journalism have grown. Whether or not suppressing scrutiny was the law’s stated purpose, its potential consequences are deeply troubling. A government that is confident in its integrity should welcome independent investigations, not create additional obstacles for journalists seeking to expose corruption and wrongdoing.

The real test of a privacy law is whether it protects citizens from the powerful—or gives the powerful greater protection from their citizens. India needs data protection, but it also needs a free press, transparent government, and institutions capable of holding those in power accountable.

I’m not a fan of the Hudson Institute at all, but the current Sino-Japanese relationship is in a pressure cooker. Anything could ignite at any moment if no serious effort is made to lower the temperature.

A common dynamic in East Asia is that whenever tensions arise between China, the two Koreas, and Japan, the history of World War II is brought back into the conversation. That history is particularly painful for Japan because it was both a victim and a perpetrator during the war. Unlike Germany, Japan did not go through the same process of formally confronting and apologizing for all the atrocities committed during the war.

When relations deteriorate, it is easy for China or Korea to reopen that wound and connect present-day disputes to Japan’s wartime history. I seriously doubt that, 80 years after the war, China is still simply seeking an apology. But the historical debt remains unresolved. The current Japanese government may not be directly responsible for what happened, nor is it obligated in the same way as the wartime government, but it has inherited that historical responsibility.

4. A developer usually borrows to buy land and pay for early work. Every month spent waiting for approvals or fighting appeals means more interest and property tax on land that isn’t earning anything.
5. Each additional $1,000 in impact fees raises the cost of bringing new homes to market by $1,390. The buyer then finances that amount over 30 years, so it costs them more with interest.
6. If costs rise above what buyers in an area can pay, some projects never get built. 
7. Regulation accounts for $132,000, or roughly 27%, of the average new single-family home price, up more than 40% since 2021.

The backyard barely accommodates a patio cover. There is no room to plant a tree, which, by the way, is also regulated. Most if not all trees allowed would not fit the tiny lots anyway,

The housing “shortage” is due to housing turning into a commodity to be traded and profited from. 

The problem with cutting minimum lot size in half to 5000 sq ft is that the minimum market rate unit cost won’t go down.  The commodity-driven housing market has way too much demand.  The larger homes and homes on larger lots with backyards will become even more expensive. Ultimately, these measures drive price per square foot even higher. 

My homeowner’s insurance calculates the cost each year to replace my home. It is less than 25% of the market rate if I sold the home.  

The rest is the land. And that is what has turned into a commodity for profiteers. And that has driven up the price. 

On top of that, in California, water is scarce (and will become scarcer). Highways are congested, especially at certain times of day and week. Classrooms are full and underfunded. And the California population is shrinking overall. 

We need proactive thinking that addresses the root of the housing cost problem (that’s what it is - it is not a housing shortage), not reactive panic measures that make no sense.

In my case, I was grieving over the loss of someone who's still alive but just isn't present in my life. It was difficult trying to get past the fact that someone who was supposed to be a role model turned out to be the person I would never want to become or seem like. Emotions like anger, denial, hurt, and sadness were all feelings that I constantly battled with and it was hard for my younger self to have to endure those feelings on my own while also trying to help others going through the same thing. The biggest help for me was going to therapy and speaking with a professional who knew how to guide me through my grief and the proper coping  mechanisms. Supporting a friend through a loss taught me that just showing up without trying to “fix” anything is what truly matters. comments.name: Braddock
comments.body: I’ve never been the best at handling challenge and shock in my life: I would typically throw a fit or bawl my eyes out whenever something didn’t go my way. So as I’ve grown and encountered new difficulties that come with adolescence, I’ve made it a priority to find sustainable ways to address my troubles. And while every now and then volatile emotions pour out, I always ensure I have something or someone to soothe me. In other words, despite the occasional overwhelming or frustrating situation, I’ve found ways to handle my thoughts and emotions in a productive way so that I could either solve the issue at hand or plan to resolve it in the future. One of my favorite methods is simply just taking a walk around my neighborhood and park. During the evening, when I find the time, I like to take a stroll and digest all the nature and people along the way. I make my way to the park a couple blocks down and immerse myself among the swingsets, sports fields, and descending sunset. By the time I make it back to my home, I feel a sense of refreshment, and I’m ready to tackle whatever work or problem is ahead of me.

comments.name: Bridget M
comments.body: Everyone goes through a hard time in life. Even if it looks different. Grief, one of the hardest and most shared experiences humans can have together, is also one of the most unexplained and darkest events in a lifetime. It makes you reflect on the things gone unsaid, the questions left unasked, the returning voice in your head saying “why?” In other words, grief is an event that will continue to change our way of life forever. We don’t have an explanation for it, and we probably never will. But, that doesn’t mean you can’t learn to grow and live your life after it. A thing I like to do is spend time with the people I care about the most. I continue to say yes to the hangouts, I decide to have lunch outside, I choose the walk instead of mindless scrolling. Those are small things, but those things are what get me through a moment in my life that might easily way me down, and allow me to continue on even if it’s hard.

Orphans and vile matrons, the lampooned hypocrisy of the upper classes, the wry, razor-sharp perceptions of the first-person narrators, one of whom is a hilariously precocious child, and a plot that doesn't let up. It was Mississippi Dickens, every sentence a pleasure and often a surprise. I loved it.

Do better.

comments.body: The absolute creepiest places aren't commercial haunted houses or tourist traps, but our own homes when we're left alone in the dark. In other words, real fear isn't about fake monsters, it's about our own brains turning a place where we usually feel safe into something completely terrifying. When a pitch-black hallway or a quiet staircase suddenly gives you goosebumps, your imagination fills in the gaps, proving that a familiar room going dark is way scarier than any staged horror attraction
